claim: Adult C. elegans AMsh glia engulf sensory endings of the AFD thermosensory neuron.
source: Adult C. elegans AMsh glia engulf sensory endings of the AFD thermosensory neuron by repurposing components of the conserved apoptotic corpse phagocytosis machinery.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The phosphatidylserine (PS) flippase TAT-1/ATP8A functions with glial PS-receptor PSR-1/PSR and PAT-2/α-integrin to initiate engulfment.
source: The phosphatidylserine (PS) flippase TAT-1/ATP8A functions with glial PS-receptor PSR-1/PSR and PAT-2/α-integrin to initiate engulfment.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 4, demonstrating the roles of these molecules in the engulfment process.

claim: Glial engulfment activates glial CED-10/Rac1 GTPase through the ternary GEF complex of CED-2/CrkII, CED-5/DOCK180, CED-12/ELMO.
source: This activates glial CED-10/Rac1 GTPase through the ternary GEF complex of CED-2/CrkII, CED-5/DOCK180, CED-12/ELMO.
evidence: Figure 5 provides genetic and molecular data showing that CED-2/5/12 complex acts upstream of CED-10 in the engulfment pathway.

claim: Execution of phagocytosis uses the actin-remodeler WSP-1/nWASp.
source: Execution of phagocytosis uses the actin-remodeler WSP-1/nWASp.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows that wsp-1 mutants have defects in engulfment, supporting its role in the process.

claim: Glial engulfment dynamically tracks AFD activity and is regulated by temperature.
source: This process dynamically tracks AFD activity and is regulated by temperature, the AFD sensory input.
evidence: Figure 6 shows that neuron activity mutants and temperature changes affect engulfment rates, and Figure 2E shows temperature-dependent differences in puncta accumulation.

claim: Glial CED-10 levels regulate engulfment rates downstream of neuron activity.
source: Importantly, glial CED-10 levels regulate engulfment rates downstream of neuron activity, and engulfment-defective mutants exhibit altered AFD-ending shape and thermosensory behavior.
evidence: Figure 5B shows that CED-10 overexpression increases puncta numbers, and Figure 6 demonstrates that CED-10 acts downstream of activity-regulating genes like tax-2.

claim: Engulfment-defective mutants exhibit altered AFD-ending shape and thermosensory behavior.
source: Importantly, glial CED-10 levels regulate engulfment rates downstream of neuron activity, and engulfment-defective mutants exhibit altered AFD-ending shape and thermosensory behavior.
evidence: Figure 7 shows that ced-10 mutants have elongated AFD-NRE microvilli and defective thermotaxis behavior.

claim: The adult C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous system comprises 302 neurons and 56 glial cells.
source: The nervous system of the adult Caenorhabditis elegans hermaphrodite comprises 302 neurons and 56 glial cells (Singhvi and Shaham, 2019; Sulston et al., 1983; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The AFD–NRE comprises ~45 actin-based microvilli and a single microtubule-based cilium.
source: The AFD–NRE comprises ~45 actin-based microvilli and a single microtubule-based cilium that are embedded in the AMsh glial cell.
evidence: This structural description is supported by references to previous work (Doroquez et al., 2014; Perkins et al., 1986) and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: AFD-derived glial puncta have an average size of 541 ± 145 nm along their long (yz) axis.
source: 3D super-resolution microscopy studies revealed that the average size of AFD-derived glial puncta is 541 ± 145 nm along their long (yz) axis (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A provides quantitative measurements of puncta size from super-resolution microscopy.

claim: AFD-derived glial puncta are an order of magnitude smaller than exophers (~3.8 µm in diameter).
source: These fragments are an order of magnitude smaller than recently described exophers extruded from neurons exposed to cellular stress (~3.8 µm in diameter) and larger than ciliary extracellular vesicles (~150 nm) (Chung et al., 2013; Melentijevic et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This comparison is made based on size measurements and references to previous studies on exophers and extracellular vesicles.

claim: AFD-derived glial puncta are larger than ciliary extracellular vesicles (~150 nm).
source: These fragments are an order of magnitude smaller than recently described exophers extruded from neurons exposed to cellular stress (~3.8 µm in diameter) and larger than ciliary extracellular vesicles (~150 nm) (Chung et al., 2013; Melentijevic et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This comparison is made based on size measurements and references to previous studies on exophers and extracellular vesicles.

claim: The size of AFD-derived glial puncta is of the same order of magnitude as individual AFD–NRE microvilli or cilia.
source: This size is of the same order of magnitude as the sizes of individual AFD–NRE microvilli or cilia as measured by electron microscopy (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and (Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A provide electron microscopy measurements of microvilli diameter, and a citation supports cilium measurements.

claim: Glial puncta are rarely found in embryos or early larval stages.
source: We found that these puncta are rarely found in embryos or early larval stages, but are easily detected in L4 larvae and increase in numbers during adulthood (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Figure 2C and 2D show developmental time course data of puncta accumulation.

claim: Glial puncta are easily detected in L4 larvae and increase in numbers during adulthood.
source: We found that these puncta are rarely found in embryos or early larval stages, but are easily detected in L4 larvae and increase in numbers during adulthood (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Figure 2C and 2D show developmental time course data of puncta accumulation.

claim: Approximately 65% of 1-day old adult animals expressing gcy-8:GFP raised at 20°C have AMsh glia containing >10 puncta.
source: We found that ~65% of 1-day old adult animals expressing the AFD–NRE-specific gcy-8:GFP raised at 20°C have AMsh glia containing >10 puncta, and another ~32% of animals have 1–9 puncta/glia (n = 171) (Figure 2C)
evidence: Figure 2C provides population distribution data of puncta numbers in wild-type animals.

claim: The AMsh glial cell of 1-day-old adults has on average 14 ± 1 puncta.
source: The AMsh glial cell of 1-day-old adults has on average 14 ± 1 puncta (n = 78) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Figure 2D provides quantitative data on puncta numbers in day 1 adults.

claim: Individual puncta separate from the NRE at a frequency of 0.8 ± 0.3 events/min.
source: Using time-lapse microscopy, we found that individual puncta separate from the NRE at a frequency of 0.8 ± 0.3 events/min and travel at 1.05 ± 0.1 µm/s down the glial process towards the cell body, consistent with motor–protein-dependent retrograde trafficking (quantifications of videos from n = 5 animals) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Videos 1 and 2; Maday et al., 2014; Paschal et al., 1987).
evidence: Time-lapse microscopy data from Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B provide quantitative measurements of puncta separation frequency.

claim: Puncta travel at 1.05 ± 0.1 µm/s down the glial process towards the cell body.
source: Using time-lapse microscopy, we found that individual puncta separate from the NRE at a frequency of 0.8 ± 0.3 events/min and travel at 1.05 ± 0.1 µm/s down the glial process towards the cell body, consistent with motor–protein-dependent retrograde trafficking (quantifications of videos from n = 5 animals) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Videos 1 and 2; Maday et al., 2014; Paschal et al., 1987).
evidence: Time-lapse microscopy data from Videos 1 and 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B provide quantitative measurements of puncta travel speed.

claim: Age-matched animals raised at different cultivation temperatures differ in glia puncta accumulation.
source: Finally, age-matched animals raised at different cultivation temperatures differ in glia puncta accumulation (Figure 2E).
evidence: Figure 2E shows quantitative data comparing puncta numbers in animals raised at 15°C, 20°C, and 25°C.

claim: Four AFD-microvilli-specific proteins (SRTX-1, GCY-8, GCY-18, and GCY-23) with fluorescent tags consistently show fluorescent puncta in glia.
source: To probe microvilli, we examined transgenic animals labeled with either of four AFD-microvilli-specific proteins with fluorescent tags, SRTX-1, GCY-8, GCY-18, and GCY-23 (Colosimo et al., 2004; Inada et al., 2006). We found that all four transgenic strains consistently show fluorescent puncta in glia (Figure 1, Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows data from multiple transgenic strains with different microvilli markers, all showing puncta in glia.

claim: DYF-11:GFP localizes to AFD cilia but no DYF-11:GFP puncta are found in AMsh glia.
source: To label cilia, we generated transgenic animals with the ciliary protein DYF-11/TRAF31B1 fluorescently tagged and expressed under an AFD-specific promoter and confirmed that PAFD:DYF-11:GFP localizes to AFD cilia (Figure 3B). However, we found no DYF-11:GFP puncta in AMsh glia (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A and 3B show that while DYF-11:GFP labels cilia, it does not appear as puncta in glia.

claim: ttx-1(p767) mutants lack AFD–NRE puncta in AMsh glia.
source: The development of AFD, including its microvilli (but not cilia), requires the terminal selector transcription factor TTX-1/Otx1/orthodenticle (Hobert, 2016; Satterlee et al., 2001). We found that ttx-1(p767) mutants lack AFD–NRE puncta in AMsh glia (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Figure 3C-E shows that ttx-1 mutants, which lack microvilli, have no puncta in glia.

claim: dyf-11(mn392) and osm-6(p811) cilia-defective mutants have glia puncta present.
source: In contrast to ttx-1 mutants, glia puncta were present in animals mutant for either dyf-11(mn392) or osm-6(p811) (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Figure 3C-E shows that cilia-defective mutants still have puncta in glia.

claim: dyf-11 cilia-defective mutants accumulate more glial puncta than wild-type animals.
source: In fact and on the contrary, we found that dyf-11 cilia-defective mutants accumulate more glial puncta that wild-type animals (dyf-11: 38 ± 3 puncta, n = 27 vs. wild type: 14 ± 1, n = 78, Figure 3C, E; and a larger fraction of dyf-11 and osm-6 mutants exhibit >10 puncta/glia [dyf-11: 95%, n = 61 animals, osm-6: 100% animals, n = 82, vs. wild type: 65%, n = 171]; Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3C-E provides quantitative data showing increased puncta in dyf-11 mutants compared to wild type.

claim: The observed puncta in AMsh glia derive from AFD–NRE microvilli as the primary, if not sole, source.
source: Data from all these approaches taken together suggest that that the observed puncta in AMsh glia derive from AFD–NRE microvilli as the primary, if not sole, source.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence from Figures 1-3, including marker localization, mutant analysis, and ablation experiments.

claim: Mutations in ced-8 do not affect glial NRE uptake.
source: PS exposure in apoptotic cells is promoted partially by the Xkr8 factor CED-8, which is cleaved by the caspase CED-3 to promote PS presentation for cell corpse phagocytosis (Bevers and Williamson, 2016; Wang et al., 2007). However, mutations in neither ced-8 (Figure 4B) nor ced-3 (data not shown) affect glial NRE uptake.
evidence: Figure 4B shows that ced-8 mutants have similar puncta levels to wild type.

claim: Mutations in ced-3 do not affect glial NRE uptake.
source: PS exposure in apoptotic cells is promoted partially by the Xkr8 factor CED-8, which is cleaved by the caspase CED-3 to promote PS presentation for cell corpse phagocytosis (Bevers and Williamson, 2016; Wang et al., 2007). However, mutations in neither ced-8 (Figure 4B) nor ced-3 (data not shown) affect glial NRE uptake.
evidence: The text states that ced-3 mutations do not affect uptake, though the data is not shown in figures.

claim: Mutations in scrm-1 only mildly decrease AFD–NRE engulfment.
source: Likewise, mutations in scrm-1, encoding a scramblase-promoting PS exposure (Wang et al., 2007), only mildly decrease AFD–NRE engulfment (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows that scrm-1 mutants have a mild reduction in puncta compared to wild type.

claim: A presumptive null mutation in tat-1 results in increased AFD–NRE engulfment.
source: However, a presumptive null mutation in tat-1, an ortholog of mammalian translocase ATP8A required for PS sequestration to the plasma membrane inner leaflet (Andersen et al., 2016), results in increased apoptotic cell corpse engulfment (Darland-Ransom et al., 2008; Hong et al., 2004) and AFD–NRE engulfment (Figure 4B, E).
evidence: Figure 4B and 4E show that tat-1 mutants have significantly increased puncta compared to wild type.

claim: Re-expression of wild-type tat-1 cDNA under an AFD-specific promoter fully rescues the tat-1 engulfment defect.
source: Importantly, re-expression of wild-type tat-1 cDNA under an AFD-specific promoter fully rescues the tat-1 engulfment defect (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows that AFD-specific expression of TAT-1 rescues the tat-1 mutant phenotype.

claim: Cell-autonomous function of the PS-flippase TAT-1 in the AFD neuron regulates engulfment of AFD–NRE fragments by AMsh glia.
source: We conclude that cell-autonomous function of the PS-flippase TAT-1 in the AFD neuron regulates engulfment of AFD–NRE fragments by AMsh glia.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the rescue experiment showing AFD-specific expression of TAT-1 rescues the mutant phenotype.

claim: Two independent ced-1 loss-of-function alleles do not block NRE fragment uptake.
source: CED-1/Draper/MEGF10 is required for removal of neuron debris in many contexts (Cherra and Jin, 2016; Mangahas and Zhou, 2005; Nichols et al., 2016), including by glia in other species (Chung et al., 2013; Freeman, 2015; Hamon et al., 2006; Raiders et al., 2021). Surprisingly, two independent ced-1 loss-of-function alleles do not block NRE fragment uptake (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows that ced-1 mutants still have puncta in glia, indicating that CED-1 is not required for uptake.

claim: Disrupting CED-6/GULP and CED-7/ABCA1 does not block engulfment.
source: Similarly, disrupting CED-6/GULP and CED-7/ABCA1, which function with CED-1/MEGF10 in C. elegans apoptotic phagocytosis and in other species (Flannagan et al., 2012; Hamon et al., 2006; Morizawa et al., 2017; Reddien and Horvitz, 2004; Zhou et al., 2001), does not block engulfment either (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows that ced-6 and ced-7 mutants still have puncta in glia.

claim: Deletion of psr-1 dramatically reduces AFD–NRE engulfment by AMsh glia.
source: Loss of the conserved phosphatidylserine receptor PSR-1/PSR has defects in apoptotic cell corpse engulfment in C. elegans and zebrafish (Hong et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2003). Remarkably, deletion of psr-1 dramatically reduces AFD–NRE engulfment by AMsh glia (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: Figure 4D and 4E show that psr-1 mutants have significantly reduced puncta compared to wild type.

claim: Expression of the PSR-1C long isoform in AMsh glia rescues psr-1 mutant defects significantly.
source: Expression of the PSR-1C long isoform in AMsh glia rescues psr-1 mutant defects significantly (Figure 4D), suggesting that PSR-1 acts in glia to promote NRE uptake.
evidence: Figure 4D shows that glial-specific expression of PSR-1 rescues the psr-1 mutant phenotype.

claim: PSR-1 acts in glia to promote NRE uptake.
source: Expression of the PSR-1C long isoform in AMsh glia rescues psr-1 mutant defects significantly (Figure 4D), suggesting that PSR-1 acts in glia to promote NRE uptake.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the glial-specific rescue experiment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A GFP:PSR-1 translational reporter expressed under an AMsh-glia-specific promoter localizes to glial membranes, including those around AFD–NRE microvilli.
source: Consistent with this function, a GFP:PSR-1 translational reporter expressed under an AMsh-glia-specific promoter localizes to glial membranes, including those around AFD–NRE microvilli (Figure 4F, F').
evidence: Figure 4F and F' show fluorescence microscopy images of GFP:PSR-1 localization in AMsh glia.

claim: PSR-1 acts downstream of TAT-1.
source: If PSR-1 recognizes PS on AFD–NRE membranes to mediate engulfment, we reasoned it should act downstream of TAT-1. We therefore constructed and analyzed psr-1; tat-1 double mutants. Unlike tat-1 single mutants that show increased NRE engulfment, psr-1; tat-1 animals exhibit reduced engulfment similar to psr-1 single mutants (Figure 4D). Thus, PSR-1 acts downstream of TAT-1.
evidence: Figure 4D shows epistasis analysis indicating that psr-1; tat-1 double mutants phenocopy psr-1 single mutants.

claim: A mutation in ttr-52 reduces NRE uptake to a similar extent as mutations in psr-1.
source: The transthyretin protein TTR-52 mediates binding between PS and PSR-1 (Neumann et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2010). Supporting the PSR-1 results, we found that a mutation in ttr-52 also reduces NRE uptake to a similar extent as mutations in psr-1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D shows that ttr-52 mutants have reduced puncta similar to psr-1 mutants.

claim: psr-1; ttr-52 double mutants show no significant enhancement of puncta defects compared to either single mutant.
source: In addition, we found that psr-1; ttr-52 double mutants show no significant enhancement of puncta defects compared to either single mutant, suggesting that PSR-1 and TTR-52 function within the same pathway for PS recognition by AMsh glia (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D shows epistasis analysis indicating that psr-1 and ttr-52 function in the same pathway.

claim: PSR-1 and TTR-52 function within the same pathway for PS recognition by AMsh glia.
source: In addition, we found that psr-1; ttr-52 double mutants show no significant enhancement of puncta defects compared to either single mutant, suggesting that PSR-1 and TTR-52 function within the same pathway for PS recognition by AMsh glia (Figure 4D).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the genetic epistasis analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A mutation in ina-1 has no effect on NRE engulfment.
source: Integrins function with MeRTK to promote photoreceptor cell outer segment engulfment by retinal RPE glia (Mao and Finnemann, 2012), and the C. elegans genome encodes two α-integrin subunits, INA-1 and PAT-2, both of which are implicated in apoptotic cell phagocytosis in C. elegans (Hsieh et al., 2012; Neukomm et al., 2014; Sáenz-Narciso et al., 2016). We found that while a mutation in ina-1 has no effect on NRE engulfment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), loss of PAT-2 by RNA interference (RNAi) significantly blocks AFD–NRE phagocytosis (Figure 4G).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows that ina-1 mutants have normal puncta levels.

claim: Loss of PAT-2 by RNA interference significantly blocks AFD–NRE phagocytosis.
source: We found that while a mutation in ina-1 has no effect on NRE engulfment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), loss of PAT-2 by RNA interference (RNAi) significantly blocks AFD–NRE phagocytosis (Figure 4G).
evidence: Figure 4G shows that pat-2 RNAi reduces puncta in wild-type animals.

claim: pat-2 RNAi strongly enhances glia engulfment defects of psr-1 mutants.
source: Further, pat-2 RNAi strongly enhances glia engulfment defects of psr-1 mutants (Figure 4G).
evidence: Figure 4G shows that pat-2 RNAi in psr-1 mutants results in a more severe reduction in puncta than either perturbation alone.

claim: PAT-2/α-integrin and PSR-1 appear to act together for glial engulfment of AFD–NRE.
source: Thus, PAT-2/α-integrin and PSR-1 appear to act together for glial engulfment of AFD–NRE.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: ced-1(e1754) strong loss-of-function mutant animals exhibit enhanced puncta numbers compared to wild-type animals.
source: Curiously, not only do mutations in ced-1 not block the appearance of puncta in glia, we found that ced-1(e1754) strong loss-of-function mutant animals actually exhibit enhanced puncta numbers compared to wild-type animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: Figure 4C shows that ced-1 mutants have more puncta than wild type.

claim: Animals bearing mutations in ced-2, ced-5, or ced-12 exhibit reduced AFD–NRE puncta in AMsh glia.
source: The ternary complex of CED-2/CrkII, CED-5/DOCK1, and CED-12/ELMO1 acts downstream of PSR-1 for apoptotic cell engulfment (Reddien and Horvitz, 2004; Wang et al., 2003). We found that animals bearing mutations in ced-2, ced-5, or ced-12 exhibit reduced AFD–NRE puncta in AMsh glia (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows that ced-2, ced-5, and ced-12 mutants all have reduced puncta compared to wild type.

claim: Expression of the CED-12B isoform in AMsh glia is sufficient to rescue ced-12 mutant defects.
source: Furthermore, expression of the CED-12B isoform in AMsh glia is sufficient to rescue ced-12 mutant defects (Figure 5A).
evidence: Figure 5A shows that glial-specific expression of CED-12 rescues the ced-12 mutant phenotype.

claim: The CED-2/CED-5/CED-12 complex likely regulates engulfment of AFD–NREs.
source: We conclude, therefore, that the CED-2/CED-5/CED-12 complex also likely regulates engulfment of AFD–NREs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mutant and rescue data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Two loss-of-function mutations in ced-10 block nearly all engulfment of AFD–NRE fragments by AMsh glia.
source: We found that two loss-of-function mutations in ced-10, or overexpression of dominant-negative CED-10T17N, block nearly all engulfment of AFD–NRE fragments by AMsh glia (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Figure 5B-D shows that ced-10 mutants have very few puncta in glia.

claim: Overexpression of dominant-negative CED-10T17N blocks nearly all engulfment of AFD–NRE fragments by AMsh glia.
source: We found that two loss-of-function mutations in ced-10, or overexpression of dominant-negative CED-10T17N, block nearly all engulfment of AFD–NRE fragments by AMsh glia (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows that expression of dominant-negative CED-10 blocks puncta formation.

claim: psr-1; ced-10 and ced-12; ced-10 double mutants show strong defects in puncta numbers reminiscent of ced-10 single mutants.
source: To determine how CED-10 functions with respect to CED-2/CED-5/CED-12 and PSR-1, we generated psr-1; ced-10 and ced-12; ced-10 double mutants. Both strains show strong defects in puncta numbers reminiscent of ced-10 single mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows epistasis analysis indicating that ced-10 is epistatic to psr-1 and ced-12.

claim: Transgenic expression of CED-10 is sufficient to overcome the partial loss of NRE engulfment in psr-1 mutants.
source: Furthermore, transgenic expression of CED-10 is sufficient to overcome the partial loss of NRE engulfment in psr-1 mutants (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows that CED-10 overexpression in psr-1 mutants increases puncta numbers.

claim: CED-10/Rac1 GTPase likely functions in glia downstream of CED-2/CED-5/CED-12 and PSR-1 to promote AMsh glial engulfment of NREs.
source: Our data are consistent with the interpretation that, like in cell corpse engulfment, CED-10/Rac1 GTPase likely functions in glia downstream of CED-2/CED-5/CED-12 and PSR-1, to promote AMsh glial engulfment of NREs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on epistasis analysis shown in Figure 5E and comparison to known apoptotic phagocytosis pathways.

claim: Mutations in unc-73/TRIO do not affect NRE uptake.
source: This activation is specific as mutations in another CED-10 activator, UNC-73/TRIO, do not affect NRE uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Lundquist et al., 2001; Sáenz-Narciso et al., 2016).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows that unc-73 mutants have normal puncta levels.

claim: Expression of constitutive active CED-10G12V results in reduced engulfed puncta.
source: Unexpectedly, expression of constitutive active CED-10G12V also results in reduced engulfed puncta (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows that expression of constitutively active CED-10 reduces puncta numbers.

claim: The AFD–NRE is significantly shorter in CED-10G12V mutants.
source: Supporting the latter model, the AFD–NRE is significantly shorter in CED-10G12V mutants (see below).
evidence: This refers to data shown later in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, which shows shortened NRE in CED-10G12V animals.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type CED-10, but not of wild-type PSR-1 or CED-12, increases NRE engulfment.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of wild-type CED-10, but not of wild-type PSR-1 or CED-12, increases NRE engulfment Figure 4D, Figure 5A,D).
evidence: Figures 4D and 5A,D show that only CED-10 overexpression, not PSR-1 or CED-12, increases puncta numbers.

claim: Glial CED-10 is both necessary and sufficient to regulate the rate at which AMsh glial engulf AFD–NRE fragments.
source: Glial CED-10 is, therefore, both necessary and sufficient to regulate the rate at which AMsh glial engulf AFD–NRE fragments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on loss-of-function, rescue, and overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Animals bearing a loss-of-function mutation in wsp-1 show a block in NRE engulfment.
source: During apoptotic cell engulfment, CED-10 executes phagocytic arm extension by mediating actin remodeling (Wang and Yang, 2016). We, therefore, examined animals bearing a loss-of-function mutation in wsp-1, which encodes an actin polymerization factor, and found a block in NRE engulfment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows that wsp-1 mutants have reduced puncta.

claim: Increasing levels of WSP-1 specifically in AMsh glia leads to increased NRE engulfment.
source: As with overexpression of CED-10, increasing levels of WSP-1 specifically in AMsh glia also lead to increased NRE engulfment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows that WSP-1 overexpression in glia increases puncta numbers.

claim: CED-10-dependent actin remodeling is the rate-limiting step for the engulfment of AFD–NREs by glia.
source: These results suggest that CED-10-dependent actin remodeling is the rate-limiting step for the engulfment of AFD–NREs by glia.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that both CED-10 and WSP-1 overexpression increase engulfment rates.

claim: Cyclic-nucleotide-gated (CNG) ion channels localize to the AFD cilium base and are required for AFD neuron firing in response to temperature stimuli.
source: Previous studies showed that cyclic-nucleotide-gated (CNG) ion channels localize to the AFD cilium base and are required for AFD neuron firing in response to temperature stimuli (Cho et al., 2004; Ramot et al., 2008; Satterlee et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: CNG channels are mis-localized in cilia-defective mutants.
source: These channels are mis-localized in cilia-defective mutants (Nguyen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: Cilia-defective mutants exhibit deficits in thermotaxis behavior.
source: Independently, it has been shown that cilia-defective mutants exhibit deficits in thermotaxis behavior (Tan et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work.

claim: tax-2 mutant glia accumulate extra puncta.
source: We examined animals defective in TAX-2, the sole CNG β-subunit in the C. elegans genome, or in TAX-4 and CNG-3, α-subunits that function together in AFD (Cho et al., 2004; Hellman and Shen, 2011; Satterlee et al., 2004) for engulfment defects. Glia in mutant animals accumulate extra puncta (tax-2: 28.1 ± 2 puncta, n = 37; tax-4; cng-3 double mutants: 23.8 ± 2.3 puncta, n = 17) (Figure 6A–C)
evidence: Figure 6A-C shows that tax-2 and tax-4; cng-3 mutants have increased puncta compared to wild type.

claim: tax-4; cng-3 double mutant glia accumulate extra puncta.
source: We examined animals defective in TAX-2, the sole CNG β-subunit in the C. elegans genome, or in TAX-4 and CNG-3, α-subunits that function together in AFD (Cho et al., 2004; Hellman and Shen, 2011; Satterlee et al., 2004) for engulfment defects. Glia in mutant animals accumulate extra puncta (tax-2: 28.1 ± 2 puncta, n = 37; tax-4; cng-3 double mutants: 23.8 ± 2.3 puncta, n = 17) (Figure 6A–C)
evidence: Figure 6A-C shows that tax-2 and tax-4; cng-3 mutants have increased puncta compared to wild type.

claim: In tax-2 mutants, a larger fraction of the animal population has >10 puncta compared to wild type.
source: and in tax-2 mutants, a larger fraction of the animal population has >10 puncta (tax-2, 99%, n = 92 animals; wild type, 65%, n = 171 animals) (Figure 6C).
evidence: Figure 6C shows population distribution data comparing tax-2 mutants to wild type.

claim: pde-1; pde-5 double mutant animals have reduced glia puncta numbers compared to wild type.
source: Conversely, we assessed the consequence of increasing the levels of cGMP, which promotes CNG channel opening, by mutating the cGMP degrading enzymes PDE-1 and PDE-5 expressed in AFD neurons (Ramot et al., 2008; Singhvi et al., 2016). We found that pde-1; pde-5 double mutant animals have reduced glia puncta numbers compared to wild type (7.1 ± 1.4, n = 11 vs. 14 ± 1, n = 78) (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Figure 6B and 6C show that pde-1; pde-5 mutants have fewer puncta than wild type.

claim: Acute and cell-specific chemogenetic silencing of AFD leads to puncta enrichment in AMsh glia within 24 hr.
source: Finally, acute and cell-specific chemogenetic silencing of AFD using a histamine-gated chloride channel (Pokala et al., 2014) expressed under an AFD-specific promoter leads to puncta enrichment in AMsh glia within 24 hr (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: Figure 6E and 6F show that histamine treatment of animals expressing HisCl1 in AFD increases puncta in glia.

claim: AFD activity levels reciprocally affect AFD–NRE engulfment levels.
source: Thus, AFD activity levels reciprocally affect AFD–NRE engulfment levels and can do so acutely.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined data from activity mutants and chemogenetic silencing experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: The increase in puncta number seen in tax-2 mutant glia is entirely suppressed by loss of CED-10.
source: Accumulation of glial puncta in AFD activity mutants could result from increased engulfment rates or, alternatively, from decreased puncta degradation. We favor the former model as we found that the increase in puncta number seen in tax-2 mutant glia is entirely suppressed by loss of CED-10 (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Figure 6B and 6C show that tax-2; ced-10 double mutants have puncta levels similar to ced-10 single mutants.

claim: Significant suppression is observed in tax-2; psr-1(tm469) double mutants compared to tax-2 alone.
source: Likewise, we also observed significant suppression in tax-2; psr-1(tm469) double mutants compared to tax-2 alone; and this suppression is enhanced further by pat-2 (RNAi) (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: Figure 6C and 6D show epistasis analysis of tax-2 with psr-1 and pat-2.

claim: Loss of ced-10 suppresses excess engulfment following acute chemogenetic silencing of AFD.
source: Loss of ced-10 also suppresses excess engulfment following acute chemogenetic silencing of AFD (Figure 6F).
evidence: Figure 6F shows that ced-10 mutants do not show increased puncta upon histamine treatment.

claim: Neuron activity controls NRE engulfment through the CED-10 pathway.
source: Our findings are therefore consistent with neuron activity controlling NRE engulfment through the CED-10 pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the epistasis experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: ced-10 loss of function results in elongated AFD–NRE microvilli.
source: We found that ced-10 loss of function, or AMsh glia-specific overexpression of dominant negative CED-10T17N, results in elongated AFD–NRE microvilli (Figure 7A, B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 7A, B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B show that ced-10 mutants have longer NRE microvilli.

claim: AMsh glia-specific overexpression of dominant negative CED-10T17N results in elongated AFD–NRE microvilli.
source: We found that ced-10 loss of function, or AMsh glia-specific overexpression of dominant negative CED-10T17N, results in elongated AFD–NRE microvilli (Figure 7A, B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 7A, B, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B show that dominant-negative CED-10 expression in glia causes longer NRE microvilli.

claim: Overexpressing wild-type CED-10 produces shorter AFD–NRE microvilli.
source: By contrast, overexpressing wild-type CED-10, which has excess puncta, produces shorter AFD–NRE microvilli, and this defect worsens with age (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Figure 7A and B show that CED-10 overexpression results in shorter NRE microvilli.

claim: The defect in AFD-NRE microvilli length from CED-10 overexpression worsens with age.
source: By contrast, overexpressing wild-type CED-10, which has excess puncta, produces shorter AFD–NRE microvilli, and this defect worsens with age (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows that the proportion of animals with defective NRE increases from day 1 to day 3 in CED-10 overexpression strains.

claim: Overexpressing GTP-locked CED10G12V leads to shorter AFD–NRE microvilli.
source: Furthermore, overexpressing GTP-locked CED10G12V also leads to shorter AFD–NRE microvilli even though it paradoxically has reduced number of puncta in glia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B show that constitutively active CED-10 expression results in shorter NRE microvilli.

claim: AMsh glial engulfment of NRE fragments is important for regulating the AFD–NRE microvilli length.
source: Thus, AMsh glial engulfment of NRE fragments is important for regulating the AFD–NRE microvilli length.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation between engulfment levels and NRE length shown in Figure 7.

claim: C. elegans seek their temperature of cultivation (Tc) when placed on a temperature gradient.
source: When placed on a temperature gradient, C. elegans seek their temperature of cultivation, Tc (Hedgecock and Russell, 1975; Figure 7C–F, wild-type data in black line).
evidence: This is a well-established behavior supported by citations and shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: This animal behavior depends on thermosensory transduction at the AFD–NRE.
source: This animal behavior depends on thermosensory transduction at the AFD–NRE (Goodman and Sengupta, 2018; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work on thermotaxis behavior.

claim: Animals with defects in AFD–NRE shape exhibit defects in thermosensory behavior.
source: Previous studies have shown that animals with defects in AFD–NRE shape also exhibit defects in this thermosensory behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: ced-10 mutants exhibit altered thermosensory behavior.
source: Consistent with this, we found that ced-10 mutants exhibit altered thermosensory behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the thermotaxis assay data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: While wild-type animals reared at 25°C migrate to their Tc = 25°C on a linear temperature gradient, ced-10 mutants prefer cooler temperatures.
source: While wild-type animals reared at 25°C migrate to their Tc = 25°C on a linear temperature gradient, ced-10 mutants prefer cooler temperatures (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: Figure 7C and D show thermotaxis behavior data comparing wild type and ced-10 mutants.

claim: Animals carrying integrated transgenes overexpressing CED-10 only in AMsh glia exhibit athermotactic defects regardless of the cultivation temperatures.
source: Furthermore, animals carrying integrated transgenes overexpressing CED-10 only in AMsh glia also exhibit athermotactic defects regardless of the cultivation temperatures (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: Figure 7E and F show thermotaxis behavior data for CED-10 overexpression strains at different cultivation temperatures.

claim: AFD–NRE engulfment by AMsh glia is required for appropriate animal thermotaxis behaviors.
source: We conclude, therefore, that AFD–NRE engulfment by AMsh glia is required for appropriate animal thermotaxis behaviors.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation between engulfment defects and behavioral defects shown in Figure 7.

claim: The athermotactic behavior of CED-10 overexpression strains mimics similar defects of tax-2 or tax-2; tax-4 double mutant animals.
source: The behavior defects we observed are consistent with the thesis that reduced neuron activity drives glial engulfment. The athermotactic behavior of CED-10 overexpression strains mimics similar defects of tax-2 or tax-2; tax-4 double mutant animals, and both manipulations lead to increased puncta and reduced neuron activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C, D; Cho et al., 2004; Satterlee et al., 2004).
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D show thermotaxis behavior data for tax-2 and tax-4 mutants, and citations support the connection to neuron activity.

claim: The cryophilic behavior of ced-10 mutants is similar to that observed in other mutants with increased AFD cGMP levels.
source: Likewise, the cryophilic behavior of ced-10 mutants, which have reduced glia puncta, is similar to that observed in other mutants with increased AFD cGMP levels (Singhvi et al., 2016).
evidence: This comparison is based on the thermotaxis data in Figure 7 and a citation to previous work on cGMP mutants.

claim: Activity-dependent glial engulfment of NRE is one mechanism by which AMsh glia and AFD coordinate regulation of NRE shape and animal thermosensory behavior.
source: We favor the model that activity-dependent glial engulfment of NRE is one mechanism by which AMsh glia and AFD coordinate regulation of NRE shape and animal thermosensory behavior.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined data from Figures 6 and 7.

claim: C. elegans glia share molecular, morphological, and functional features with vertebrate sense-organ glia and astrocytes.
source: Glia of the nematode C. elegans share molecular, morphological, and functional features with vertebrate sense-organ glia and astrocytes (Bacaj et al., 2008a; Katz et al., 2018; Katz et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2021; Singhvi and Shaham, 2019; Wallace et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Glial CED-10 levels dictate engulfment rates.
source: Exploiting unique features of our experimental model, we demonstrate that glial CED-10 levels dictate engulfment rates, revealing that glia drive neuronal remodeling and do not just passively clear shed neuronal debris.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 5 showing that CED-10 overexpression increases engulfment and loss-of-function decreases it.

claim: Glia drive neuronal remodeling and do not just passively clear shed neuronal debris.
source: Exploiting unique features of our experimental model, we demonstrate that glial CED-10 levels dictate engulfment rates, revealing that glia drive neuronal remodeling and do not just passively clear shed neuronal debris.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the finding that glial CED-10 levels control engulfment rates and NRE shape.

claim: Engulfment is required for post-developmental maintenance of sensory NRE shape and behavior.
source: Indeed, we demonstrate that engulfment is required for post-developmental maintenance of sensory NRE shape and behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 7 showing that engulfment defects lead to altered NRE shape and behavior in adults.

claim: Glial engulfment extends a role for glial engulfment in the active sensory perception of temperature.
source: This also extends a role for glial engulfment in the active sensory perception of temperature.
evidence: This is based on the finding that engulfment affects thermosensory behavior shown in Figure 7.

claim: Pruning of individual neurons by a single glia modifies animal behavior.
source: Importantly, our studies allow us to directly demonstrate at single-cell resolution that pruning of individual neurons by a single glia modifies animal behavior.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between glial engulfment of AFD and thermotaxis behavior shown in Figure 7.

claim: Phagocytosis is impacted by neuronal activity states.
source: This, in conjunction with our finding that phagocytosis is impacted by neuronal activity states, demonstrates important physiological relevance.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6 showing that neuron activity mutants have altered engulfment.

claim: Glia-dependent phagocytosis can be dynamically tuned throughout animal life to modulate NRE morphology, impacting animal behavior.
source: Our studies reveal a fundamental distinction between glia-dependent phagocytosis and other modes of engulfment. Apoptotic cell phagocytosis, glial clearance of injury-induced neuronal debris, and related engulfment events are all-or-none phenomena: engulfment either occurs or does not. By contrast, we show here that in AMsh glia engulfment rate is dynamically tuned throughout animal life to modulate NRE morphology, impacting animal behavior.
evidence: This is based on the developmental time course data in Figure 2 and the activity-dependent regulation shown in Figure 6.

claim: Controlled phagocytosis may similarly regulate glial engulfment in other settings.
source: The molecular parallels between the engulfment machinery in the peripheral sense-organ AMsh glia and other CNS glial engulfment lead us to posit that controlled phagocytosis may similarly regulate glial engulfment in other settings.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the molecular conservation of the engulfment pathway.

claim: Apoptotic phagocytosis in C. elegans relies predominantly on CED-1, with the PS-receptor PSR-1 playing a minor role.
source: Apoptotic phagocytosis in C. elegans relies predominantly on CED-1, with the PS-receptor PSR-1 playing a minor role (Wang et al., 2003; Wang and Yang, 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: CED-1 is dispensable for pruning by AMsh glia.
source: Surprisingly, while CED-1 is dispensable for pruning by AMsh glia, we identified PSR-1/PS-receptor as a novel regulator of glial pruning.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4C showing that ced-1 mutants still have puncta in glia.

claim: PSR-1/PS-receptor is a novel regulator of glial pruning.
source: Surprisingly, while CED-1 is dispensable for pruning by AMsh glia, we identified PSR-1/PS-receptor as a novel regulator of glial pruning.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 4D-E showing that psr-1 mutants have reduced puncta.

claim: Engulfment of small cell process debris of the C. elegans tail-spike cell is independent of CED-1.
source: One possibility is that this difference in receptors reflects the size of particles engulfed. Supporting this notion, engulfment of small cell process debris of the C. elegans tail-spike cell is also independent of CED-1 (Ghose et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work on tail-spike cell debris engulfment.

claim: Other PS-receptors that regulate glial engulfment across species include CED-1/MEGF10/Draper, MerTK, and GPR56.
source: Other PS-receptors that have been shown to regulate glial engulfment across species include CED-1/MEGF10/Draper, MerTK, and GPR56, and it is likely that yet others await identification (Chung et al., 2013; Freeman, 2015; Hilu-Dadia and Kurant, 2020; Kevany and Palczewski, 2010; Li et al., 2020; Nomura-Komoike et al., 2020; Raiders et al., 2021; Tasdemir-Yilmaz and Freeman, 2014; Vecino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Murine P4-ATPases ATP8A1 and ATP8A2 are expressed in the nervous system.
source: We note that murine P4-ATPases ATP8A1 and ATP8A2 are expressed in the nervous system, and knockout mice exhibit deficient hippocampal learning, sensory deficits, cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, and spinal cord degeneration, and shortened photoreceptor NRE length (Coleman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work on murine ATP8A knockout mice.

claim: Murine ATP8A knockout mice exhibit deficient hippocampal learning, sensory deficits, cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, spinal cord degeneration, and shortened photoreceptor NRE length.
source: We note that murine P4-ATPases ATP8A1 and ATP8A2 are expressed in the nervous system, and knockout mice exhibit deficient hippocampal learning, sensory deficits, cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, and spinal cord degeneration, and shortened photoreceptor NRE length (Coleman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work on murine ATP8A knockout mice.

claim: TTR-52 is implicated in apoptotic phagocytosis and nerve regeneration.
source: We also identify the PS bridging molecule TTR-52 as a regulator of pruning. It is also implicated in apoptotic phagocytosis and nerve regeneration (Neumann et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work on TTR-52 function.

claim: Retinal RPE glia and cortical astrocytes require PS-bridging opsonins (Gas6 and MFGE8) to engulf neuron fragments.
source: Retinal RPE glia and cortical astrocytes also require PS-bridging opsonins (Gas6 and MFGE8) to engulf neuron fragments (Bellesi et al., 2017; Kevany and Palczewski, 2010).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work on opsonins in mammalian glia.

claim: Aberrantly excessive/reduced pruning correlate with disease in mammals.
source: Aberrantly excessive/reduced pruning correlate with disease in mammals, hinting that similar subcellular precision in marking fragments/endings for engulfment might be involved (Chung et al., 2015; Wilton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous work on pruning defects in disease.

claim: Peripheral glia of the inner ear activate phagocytosis only in injury settings.
source: Peripheral glia of the inner ear are known to activate phagocytosis only in injury settings (Bird et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work on inner ear glia.

claim: Glial pruning is conserved in both CNS and PNS and is executed for normal neural functions by analogous molecular mechanisms.
source: Our studies demonstrate that pruning of sensory neuron endings by glia is required for accurate sensory perception. Thus, glial pruning is conserved in both CNS and PNS and is executed for normal neural functions by analogous molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the findings that AMsh glia (PNS) use similar molecular machinery to CNS glia for pruning.

claim: AMsh glia and AFD neuron cooperate through multiple mechanisms to regulate AFD–NRE shape and animal thermosensory behaviors.
source: While these studies identify glial pruning as a mechanism to control NRE shape in response to activity states, we note that it is likely that AMsh glia and AFD neuron cooperate through multiple mechanisms to regulate AFD–NRE shape and animal thermosensory behaviors, including some that we previously identified (Singhvi et al., 2016; Wallace et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the current findings combined with citations to previous work from the same group.

claim: Appropriate thermosensory behaviors are critical for animal survival.
source: Such regulatory complexity might reflect the fact that appropriate thermosensory behaviors are critical for animal survival.
evidence: This is a speculation based on general biological knowledge about the importance of sensory behaviors.

claim: Glial CED-10 levels can modulate engulfment rates, NRE shape, and animal behavior.
source: Three lines of evidence in this study lead us to conclude that AMsh glia actively drive engulfment rather than passively clearing debris. (1) Our finding that glial CED-10 levels can modulate engulfment rates, NRE shape, and animal behavior suggests that this process can be triggered by glia.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 5 and 7 showing that CED-10 levels affect engulfment, NRE shape, and behavior.

claim: Short NRE shape can derive from independent mechanisms.
source: (2) While both CED-10 overexpression and ttx-1 mutants have short NRE (Satterlee et al., 2001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), unlike animals overexpressing CED-10, ttx-1 mutants have fewer puncta, not more (Figure 2A). Thus, short NRE shape can derive from independent mechanisms.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparing the phenotypes of CED-10 overexpression and ttx-1 mutants.

claim: Engulfment tracks neuron activity.
source: Furthermore, that engulfment tracks neuron activity and modulating this process impacts animal behavior also suggests a physiological role for this process.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 6 showing that activity mutants have altered engulfment.

claim: Modulating engulfment impacts animal behavior.
source: Furthermore, that engulfment tracks neuron activity and modulating this process impacts animal behavior also suggests a physiological role for this process.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 7 showing that engulfment defects alter thermotaxis behavior.

claim: Glial engulfment is an active regulator of neural functions.
source: In summary, our findings reveal glial engulfment as an active regulator of neural functions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Engulfment may be a general mechanism by which glia dynamically modulate sensory perception and neural functions, across modalities, systems, and species.
source: This raises the possibility that engulfment may be a general mechanism by which glia dynamically modulate sensory perception and neural functions, across modalities, systems, and species.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in C. elegans and the conservation of the molecular machinery.
